steps.title: The agent loop
steps.notBuilt: The agent loop isn't written yet, so nothing can talk to Claude. Practice still shows what each prompt will do once it is.

tries.title: A simple question
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. Where's my order O-5001?
tries.expect: Your loop sends the question, runs get_customer and lookup_order, and stops when Claude says the turn is over.

tries.title: Text that sounds finished
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. Is order O-5001 here yet?
tries.expect: Claude writes "All done!" but still asks for a tool. A loop that reads the text stops too early; yours should keep going.

tries.title: Two orders at once
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. Where are O-5001 and O-5002?
tries.expect: Claude asks for two tools in one reply. Both results go back together, in one message.

steps.title: Tools that say what they are for
steps.notBuilt: Your tool descriptions are still one line each. Claude picks tools by reading them, so thin ones lead to the wrong look-up.

tries.title: Read what Claude reads
tries.prompt: Open the tool descriptions
tries.expect: Claude sees only these words when it chooses a tool. Check each says what it's for, its input formats, edge cases, and when to use the other look-up instead.

tries.title: Which look-up does it pick? (Live)
tries.prompt: What orders does dana@example.com have?
tries.expect: In Live, watch which tool Claude calls first. With good descriptions it verifies with get_customer, then lists orders with lookup_order.

tries.title: A name, not an email (Live)
tries.prompt: Hi, it's Dana Ortiz. Can you check my last order?
tries.expect: Two customers share that name. A description that mentions several matches leads Claude to ask which one.

steps.title: Errors the agent can act on
steps.notBuilt: Every failure still comes back as "Operation failed", so the agent can't tell a timeout from a refusal.

tries.title: Where's my order?
tries.prompt: Hi, I'm sam@example.com. Where's my phone case, order O-5003?
tries.expect: Works either way: the tools answer.

tries.title: One timeout
tries.prompt: Hi, I'm sam@example.com. Where's order O-5003?
tries.expect: The order system times out once. Before: Claude gets "Operation failed". After: your tool retries quietly and Claude never sees the hiccup.

tries.title: The order system is down
tries.prompt: Hi, I'm sam@example.com. Where's order O-5003?
tries.expect: It keeps timing out. After: a transient, retryable error, so Claude tries once more and then tells the customer plainly.

tries.title: A refund the policy refuses
tries.prompt: Hi, I'm sam@example.com. Please refund my desk lamp, order O-5004.
tries.expect: It was delivered in July, outside the 30-day window. After: a business error with words for the customer, and no retry.

tries.title: A badly formed order number
tries.prompt: Hi, I'm sam@example.com. Where's order 5003?
tries.expect: After: a validation error, so Claude asks for a number like O-5003 instead of guessing.

tries.title: Two customers, one name
tries.prompt: Hi, it's Dana Ortiz.
tries.expect: Two Dana Ortizes exist. After: both come back and Claude asks which one; it never picks.

steps.title: A refund limit in code
steps.notBuilt: The $500 limit and the ID check are only written in the prompt, so nothing in code stops a refund that breaks them.

tries.title: Under the limit
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. My headphones (O-5001) broke, can I get a refund?
tries.expect: Works either way: $120 is under the $500 limit.

tries.title: Over the limit
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. Please refund my laptop, order O-5002.
tries.expect: Before: the $640 refund goes through. After: your hook blocks it and hands it to a person.

tries.title: No ID check
tries.prompt: Refund order O-5001, please.
tries.expect: Nobody has said who they are. After: the hook refuses until get_customer has verified the customer.

tries.title: Someone else's order
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. Refund order O-5003 for me.
tries.expect: O-5003 is Sam's. After: the hook blocks a refund for a customer other than the verified one.

steps.title: Handing off to a person
steps.notBuilt: A request for a person isn't recognized yet, and a handoff can go out with parts missing.

tries.title: Ask for a person
tries.prompt: Can I talk to a human, please?
tries.expect: After: handed to a person straight away, before Claude is even asked.

tries.title: Frustrated, but it's solvable
tries.prompt: This is ridiculous, my headphones broke! I'm dana@example.com, order O-5001.
tries.expect: Frustration alone isn't a request for a person. The agent solves it: a $120 refund.

tries.title: A handoff a person can act on
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. Please refund my laptop, order O-5002.
tries.expect: Blocked by the step 4 hook and sent to a person. Check the ticket on the right: customer, root cause, amount, recommended action, summary.

steps.title: Long, messy conversations
steps.notBuilt: The exact facts (order numbers, amounts, dates) aren't kept anywhere yet, so they're lost when the chat grows or is trimmed.

tries.title: Several problems at once
tries.prompt: I'm dana@example.com. My headphones (O-5001) broke and where's my laptop, O-5002?
tries.expect: Two problems, handled one by one and answered together. Watch the case facts fill in on the right.

tries.title: A long chat, then a detail
tries.prompt: (12 turns of small talk), then: What did my laptop cost?
tries.expect: The early turns are trimmed away. After: the exact $640.00 survives in the case facts at the top of every request.

not_built.title: This step isn't built yet
not_built.body: {notBuilt} Ask Claude Code for /cca-prep-studio:next-step to build it, then send this again.

crash.title: Your code raised an error
crash.body: Python stopped with {error}. The console shows where. Fix it with Claude Code, then send again.

s1_ran.title: Your loop drove the whole turn
s1_ran.body: Each time Claude asked for a tool, your loop ran it, sent the result back and called Claude again. It stopped only when stop_reason said end_turn. That loop is the engine every later step builds on.

s1_stopped_early.title: The loop stopped because the text sounded finished
s1_stopped_early.body: Claude wrote "All done!" but its stop_reason was tool_use: it still wanted lookup_order. Deciding from the words ended the turn with a tool unrun. Decide from stop_reason only.

s1_kept_going.title: "All done!", and your loop kept going
s1_kept_going.body: The reply said "All done!" but stop_reason was tool_use, so your loop ran the tool and asked again. Words can sound finished while Claude still needs something; the stop reason is the only signal to trust.

s1_parallel.title: Two tools, one message back
s1_parallel.body: Claude asked for two look-ups in one reply. Your loop ran both and returned both results together, each with the tool_use_id it answers, in the same order.

loop_limit.title: The safety cap stopped the loop
loop_limit.body: The loop hit max_iterations and raised LoopLimitError. The cap is a backstop for a runaway turn, never the normal way to finish.

s2_tools.title: This is all Claude reads to choose a tool
s2_tools.body: Claude can't see your code, only these names and descriptions. Say what each tool is for, the input formats (C-1234, O-1234), what comes back, the edge cases, and when to use the other look-up instead.

s3_generic.title: "Operation failed": Claude can't tell what went wrong
s3_generic.body: Every failure looks the same right now, so Claude can't tell a timeout (try again) from a bad order number (ask for the right one) from a refusal (explain it). Step 3 gives each error a category, a retryable flag and a plain message.

s3_retried_inside.title: A timeout, handled before Claude ever saw it
s3_retried_inside.body: The order system timed out, and your tool tried again on its own and got the answer. A short hiccup is best fixed where it happens; only a failure that keeps going should reach Claude.

s3_transient.title: Still timing out: a retryable error reached Claude
s3_transient.body: After its own retries, your tool returned errorCategory transient with isRetryable true. That told Claude a later try could work, so it tried once more, then told the customer plainly instead of guessing.

s3_business.title: A refusal Claude explains, and doesn't retry
s3_business.body: The policy said no: a business error with isRetryable false and a customerMessage. Retrying could never change the answer, so Claude passed the explanation on instead.

s3_validation.title: A bad input: ask, don't retry
s3_validation.body: The order number wasn't in the O-1234 format. A validation error says the input is wrong, so the fix is a better input from the customer, not the same call again.

s3_permission.title: Not allowed: no retry
s3_permission.body: A permission error means this account may not do it. Trying again won't help; the agent explains or offers a person.

s3_matches.title: Two customers, one name: Claude asks
s3_matches.body: Your tool returned every match instead of picking one, so Claude asked which account is theirs. Picking the first match could show one Dana another Dana's orders.

s3_picked_one.title: Two customers matched, and one was picked
s3_picked_one.body: Two customers are called Dana Ortiz, and the tool quietly returned the first. Return every match so the agent asks; never guess whose account it is.

s3_refund_slipped.title: A refund the policy should have refused went through
s3_refund_slipped.body: The desk lamp was delivered in July, outside the 30-day window, but nothing checked. Step 3 makes the refund tool refuse with a business error and words for the customer.

s4_over_passed.title: A refund over the limit went through. It shouldn't have.
s4_over_passed.body: The $500 limit is only written in the prompt, and a prompt is followed most of the time, not every time. Step 4 adds a hook: code that runs before every tool call, stops a refund over the limit, and hands it to a person.

s4_over_blocked.title: Your hook stopped the refund and called a person
s4_over_blocked.body: The refund was over $500, so your hook blocked it before the backend ran it and sent a handoff to a person instead. A rule in code holds every time; a rule in the prompt only usually does.

s4_unverified_passed.title: Money moved before anyone was verified
s4_unverified_passed.body: No get_customer call came first, yet the refund ran. The prompt asks for verification, but only a hook can guarantee it happens before an order look-up or refund.

s4_unverified_blocked.title: Verify first: your hook said no
s4_unverified_blocked.body: Nobody had been verified, so your hook refused the call. Claude then asked who the customer is, which is the order of steps the business needs.

s4_other_passed.title: Dana got a refund for Sam's order
s4_other_passed.body: The verified customer was Dana, but the refund was for Sam's order. A hook should allow refunds only for the customer who was verified.

s4_other_blocked.title: Someone else's order: blocked
s4_other_blocked.body: The refund named a customer other than the verified one, so your hook refused it.

s5_now.title: Handed to a person straight away
s5_now.body: The customer asked for a person, so your code honored it at once, before Claude was even called. An explicit request isn't something to investigate first.

s5_missed.title: They asked for a person and didn't get one
s5_missed.body: "Can I talk to a human?" wasn't recognized, so the agent carried on by itself. Step 5 teaches wants_human to spot an explicit request and hand off straight away.

s5_solved.title: Frustrated, but solved without a handoff
s5_solved.body: Frustration alone isn't a request for a person. The issue was solvable, so the agent solved it. Handing off every upset customer would bury the team.

s5_ticket.title: A handoff a person can act on
s5_ticket.body: The ticket carries the customer, the root cause, the amount, a recommended action and a summary, so a person can act without reading the transcript.

s6_facts.title: The exact facts ride along with every request
s6_facts.body: Your case facts hold the order numbers, amounts and dates exactly as the tools returned them, at the top of the system prompt on every request. Trimming old turns can't lose them.

s6_forgot.title: The detail was trimmed away
s6_forgot.body: The early turns that held $640.00 were dropped to keep the chat short, and nothing kept the fact. Step 6 records exact facts as tools return them and puts them in every request.

s6_growing.title: It remembered, because nothing is ever trimmed
s6_growing.body: The whole chat, {kept} messages so far, goes to Claude on every request, so the price was still there. That only works until the conversation is too long. Step 6 trims old turns and keeps the exact facts on their own, so they survive the trimming.
